research_markdown: **Caveat:** my search quota ran out after about 8 queries. Claims with a URL come from sources I retrieved. Items marked **[unverified]** are from my background knowledge and need checking before you use them in outreach or a deck. The sources imply today is roughly Q3–Q4 2026, so I treat "next 6 months" as about Oct 2026–Mar 2027. ## Market backdrop (applies to every segment) **Standard policies are closing the gap on AI.** - A secondary source (a Substack, so verify against the primary filings) reports that Berkley introduced an "absolute" AI exclusion across D&O, E&O and fiduciary lines, and AIG and Great American followed with their own filings. - The same source says Verisk's ISO form CG 40 47 01 26 removes CGL coverage for bodily injury, property damage and advertising injury arising from generative AI. - This is the main trigger for the pitch. Customers who renew into these forms will find their AI exposure uninsured. **A few affirmative products exist, so there are competitors and reinsurance partners to benchmark.** - Armilla launched affirmative AI liability cover backed by Lloyd's underwriters, and a Medium analysis cites $25M limits. - Per Armilla's press page, Chaucer and Armilla launched a combined cyber, tech E&O and AI liability structure in Feb 2026. The page also lists an A-LIGN partnership. **Regulation is a mixed picture.** - The EU Digital Omnibus moves the high-risk deadline to 2 Dec 2027 and the Annex I deadline to 2 Aug 2028, but Article 50 transparency rules still apply from Aug 2026. - Gibson Dunn confirms 2 Aug 2026 remains a live compliance date for Article 50. - Chatbots are therefore in scope now, while high-risk use cases such as HR and credit have more time. - Colorado AI Act status and federal preemption: I couldn't verify these. **[unverified]** ## Segments, ranked by 6-month purchase likelihood ### 1. Consumer companion and character chatbot platforms (highest pain, hardest to insure) - **Who:** AI companion, role-play, wellness and teen-facing chat apps (Character.AI, Replika-type apps), plus big-tech chat products. - **Why liability:** - Character.AI and Google agreed to settle the first teen chatbot harm and wrongful-death suits, including Garcia, though more families keep filing. - OpenAI and Meta have faced similar chatbot safety suits and probes. - California SB 243 took effect 1 Jan 2026. It is the first chatbot law with protections tailored to minors, and New York has a comparable law. - SB 243 requires disclosures, safety protocols and annual reporting. - **Buying signals:** a new SB 243 compliance program, minor-safety hires, a pending suit or AG inquiry, or a funding round with investor diligence on liability. - **Public examples:** Meta, Alphabet, Snap, Microsoft. The pure-plays are private. - **Channels:** trust and safety leaders, general counsel, and their venture investors. A risk assessment mapped to SB 243 is an easier first sale than a policy, because capacity for bodily-injury exposure is thin. ### 2. B2B AI SaaS vendors with copilots and agents sold to enterprises - **Who:** CX and support automation, sales and HR copilots, vertical AI SaaS. - **Why liability:** - Customers push indemnities and AI-specific warranties down the supply chain in procurement. - Tech E&O renewals are adding AI exclusions (see the backdrop above). - Affirmative products now exist, notably the Chaucer/Armilla combined cyber, tech E&O and AI structure, so buyers have something concrete to compare. - EU Article 50 applies to chatbot providers. Cooley notes it still applies from 2 Aug 2026 for new generative AI systems. - **Buying signals:** enterprise security questionnaires asking for AI coverage, SOC 2 or ISO 42001 projects, an E&O renewal with a new exclusion endorsement, and EU customer expansion. - **Public examples (my selection, not from sources):** Salesforce, ServiceNow, HubSpot, Workday, C3.ai, UiPath, SoundHound, Freshworks. Workday also faces a hiring-AI bias suit (Mobley) **[unverified]**. - **Channels:** tech E&O brokers (Marsh, Aon, WTW, and specialists such as Founder Shield or Embroker), A-LIGN-style auditors and compliance platforms (Vanta, Drata), and CISO and GC communities. Partnering with auditors is a proven route, per Armilla's A-LIGN deal. ### 3. Customer-service-heavy deployers (airlines, retail, telecom, travel) - **Who:** non-tech companies that put an LLM bot in front of customers. - **Why liability:** companies are held to what their bot says. The best-known case is Moffatt v. Air Canada (BC tribunal, 2024), which held the airline liable for its chatbot's misstatement. I did not retrieve a source this session, so I'm flagging it **[unverified]**. - Standard CGL and cyber forms now exclude generative AI. See the CG 40 47 01 26 discussion. - **Buying signals:** a public bot launch, a viral bot-error incident, risk-factor language on AI in 10-Ks, and CGL renewals with the new endorsement. - **Public examples:** Air Canada, plus large US airlines, telcos and retailers **[my selection]**. - **Channels:** corporate risk managers and large-account brokers. The sales pitch is that the CGL or E&O coverage they assume they have is gone. ### 4. Regulated-industry deployers (healthcare and mental health, fintech, insurance, legal) - **Who:** AI intake and triage bots, wellness chat, lending and support agents, legal copilots. - **Why liability:** several states regulate AI in mental health and healthcare, and sector regulators such as the CFPB and state insurance departments apply existing rules to AI. I did not retrieve sources for these, so I'm flagging them **[unverified]**. - Companion-chatbot laws such as SB 243 and New York's law will overlap with wellness products. - Professional-services AI work is called out as excluded under Berkley's wording, per the same Substack source. - **Buying signals:** compliance hires, regulator inquiries, and a model-risk or vendor-risk review of AI. - **Channels:** compliance and model-risk officers, industry associations, and regulated-sector brokers. A risk assessment tends to lead here, because these buyers already know how to buy audits. ### 5. Agentic AI and coding-agent startups (growing, not yet the top segment) - **Who:** companies shipping agents that take actions such as refunds, code changes and purchases. - **Why liability:** autonomous actions create property-damage and financial-loss exposure that sits between cyber and E&O. I did not retrieve incident sources, so I'm flagging this **[unverified]**. - **Buying signals:** enterprise pilots stalling at procurement over "who pays if the agent errs", and pursuit of an AI security or agent standard. - **Channels:** VCs and accelerators, and developer and security conferences. Expect a long cycle and a focus on assessments, because there is little loss history to price. ## What to do next - **Lead with:** segments 2 and 3. They have the clearest trigger (exclusions at renewal) and an identifiable budget owner. Use segment 1 for urgency-driven assessments. - **Priority gaps to verify:** - Colorado AI Act status. - Federal preemption of state AI laws. - Illinois, Utah and Nevada AI health laws. - The Air Canada ruling. - Agent incidents. - The Berkley and ISO filings (the Substack is secondary). - I can rerun those searches if you give me another search window.
